title: Millisecond phonon lifetimes in piezoelectric nanomechanical resonators
authors: Oliver A. Hitchcock, Matthew P. Maksymowych, Kaveh Pezeshki, Takuma Makihara, Erik Szakiel, Chou-Wei Kiang, Daniel Rugar, Amir H. Safavi-Naeini
abstract: Piezoelectric nanomechanical resonators operating at gigahertz frequencies are a promising platform for quantum information processing and precision sensing, but phonon lifetimes have been limited to the microsecond range, widely attributed to the higher intrinsic loss of piezoelectric materials. Here we show that this limitation is not fundamental. Using a fabrication process informed by recent studies of defect-mediated loss in lithium niobate, we combine chemical restoration of ion-milled surfaces with a shadow-mask metallization process to produce lithium niobate phononic crystal resonators with inferred internal phonon lifetimes of up to 21 milliseconds at 3.6 gigahertz, corresponding to quality factors exceeding $4\times10^8$ ($f\cdot Q_i > 10^{18}$) at millikelvin temperatures. By systematically varying the electrode-to-resonator spacing, we demonstrate that the measured lifetime is set by external coupling between the device and the measurement circuit rather than material loss. This establishes that lithium niobate, once fabrication-induced surface damage is removed, achieves an intrinsic quality comparable to the best mechanical materials while remaining an intrinsically piezoelectric platform with strong electromechanical coupling.
summary: This paper reports a breakthrough in the coherence of piezoelectric nanomechanical resonators using Lithium Niobate. By developing a specialized fabrication process that removes surface damage, the authors demonstrated intrinsic phonon lifetimes reaching 21 milliseconds. This proves that LN can achieve high quality factors necessary for advanced quantum sensing and information processing.
main_problem: Previous measurements of phonon lifetimes in piezoelectric nanomechanical resonators were limited to the microsecond range, leading to the incorrect assumption that high intrinsic loss was fundamental to piezoelectric materials.
main_result: By employing a novel fabrication process, the authors demonstrated intrinsic phonon lifetimes up to 21 milliseconds, proving that the limitation was due to surface damage rather than the material itself.
method: Phonon lifetime was measured using microwave reflectometry (VNA spectroscopy) by varying the electrode-to-resonator spacing to decouple external coupling losses from intrinsic material losses.
model_or_system: The study uses piezoelectric nanomechanical resonators, specifically Lithium Niobate (LN) phononic crystal resonators, operating at gigahertz frequencies. The system's performance is characterized by its electromechanical coupling and phonon coherence time.
key_observables: Phonon lifetime ($T_1$), external coupling rate ($\kappa_e$), intrinsic quality factor ($Q_i$), and the electromechanical figure of merit ($M$).
important_parameters: Resonance frequencies (3-4 GHz), temperature (mK), and electrode spacing (360 nm to 4760 nm).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption challenged is that high intrinsic loss is fundamental to piezoelectric LN; the success relies on the novel shadow-mask metallization process to remove surface damage.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phonon lifetime ringdown decay showing $T_1$ tracking the external coupling limit as electrode spacing increases, and detail the shadow-mask metallization process.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares measured phonon lifetimes ($T_1$) against external coupling limits ($T_e$) across varying electrode spacings. It then quantifies the intrinsic loss ($T_{1,in}$) achieved using a specialized fabrication technique, establishing a high figure of merit ($M$).
why_interesting: The work directly addresses the coherence time of mechanical oscillators, which is a critical component for quantum transducers and quantum memory elements, bridging solid-state physics with quantum information.

FIG. 3: Comparison of internal quality factor versus effective electromechanical coupling. Parameters are shown for this work and various other acoustic materials and platforms from the literature, with each point label corresponding to the reference number. Literature k2 eff values are simulation- or circuit-model-derived (Appendix E); for this work, the bar spans the parasitics-loaded measurement (unfilled) and the simulated intrinsic value (filled). Gray lines denote constant resonator figure of merit: M = k2 effQi/(1 −k2 eff).

FIG. 4: Microwave measurement setup. Schematic of the cryogenic wiring and room-temperature electronics used for reflectometry measurements. The device is thermalized to 10 mK at the base stage of a dilution refrigerator. The input line is attenuated to suppress thermal noise, and the output signal is amplified by a near-quantum-limited TWPA followed by a HEMT and room-temperature LNA. A VNA is used for spectroscopy and a Quantum Machines OPX for pulsed ringdown measurements.

FIG. 5: Microwave Reflectometry Measurement. The measured magnitude and phase response of a 3.35 GHz device (at 10 mK and n ≈100 phonons) with a designed electrode spacing of 2800 nm is shown as black dots. The corresponding fit of experimental data to Eq. B1 is shown as a red line, while the simulated reflection spectrum from our noisy Langevin model is shown as blue x’s.
